title: Backlit Photos: How to Shoot Into the Light Without Dark Faces — cv.cm
description: How to take backlit photos: exposure compensation and spot metering for bright faces, silhouettes, fill flash or a reflector, phone HDR and lens flare control.
h1: How do you take backlit photos without the subject turning dark?
answer: When the light is behind your subject, the camera exposes for the bright background and the face goes dark. Fix it by metering on the face (tap it on a phone, or use spot metering), adding about +1 to +2 EV of exposure compensation, or adding light to the front with a reflector or fill flash. For a silhouette, do the opposite: expose for the sky.

sections.h: What backlight is and why it fools the camera
body: Backlight means the main light source is behind the subject and in front of the camera: the sun low in the sky behind a person, a bright window behind someone indoors, or a lamp behind a glass. It can make beautiful photos: hair outlined with light, glowing leaves, warm haze and long shadows coming toward the camera.

The problem is the meter. A camera or phone measures the whole scene and tries to make it an average brightness. When most of the frame is bright sky or window, the camera darkens the exposure, and the subject, which is lit only from behind, falls into shadow. The background can be 3 to 5 stops brighter than the shaded front of a face.

You have three ways out: expose for the subject and let the background go bright, add light to the subject so the difference shrinks, or expose for the background and make the subject a silhouette on purpose. Decide which one before you shoot.

body: Silhouettes need a clear outline. Turn people sideways so the nose, chin and hands separate from the body, keep space between people, and avoid overlapping shapes. A low camera angle that puts the subject fully against the sky works best.

ol: Use aperture priority (A or Av) with a wide aperture such as f/1.8 to f/2.8 to blur the background and keep the shutter fast.
Set spot or center-weighted metering and place the spot on the face, or keep evaluative metering and add exposure compensation.
Start at +1 EV, take a shot, and check the face on the screen. Go up to +1.7 or +2 EV if the sky is very bright.
Turn on highlight warnings (blinkies). Decide which parts may go white: the sky can, the face and a white dress should not.
Focus on the near eye. Strong backlight lowers contrast and can make autofocus hunt; if it does, shade the lens with your hand or focus on an edge with more contrast.
Set white balance to daylight or shade to keep warm sunset color, or shoot RAW.
Shoot RAW if you can. It keeps more detail in the shadows and the sky for editing later.

body: With a low sun, put it just behind the subject's head or shoulder rather than in open sky. The head blocks the direct sun, the hair gets a rim of light, and the lens gets less flare.

sections.h: Add light to the front: reflector and fill flash
body: Exposure compensation brightens the face but also burns out the background. Adding light to the front keeps both.

ul: Reflector: a white or silver reflector held below and in front of the face, angled toward the sun, bounces light back. White is soft and natural; silver is stronger; gold adds warmth but can look orange. A white wall, a light-colored road or a large sheet of paper also works.

Fill flash: set the flash to TTL and use about -1 to -2 stops of flash compensation, so it only lifts shadows and does not look like flash. Keep the shutter at or below the flash sync speed, often around 1/200 s, or use high-speed sync; if needed, close the aperture or use an ND filter.
Phone flash: it is weak beyond 1 to 2 meters, but at close range it can lift a face. Try one frame with and one without.
Indoors with a window: turn the person so the window is to their side, not directly behind, or place a lamp or second window in front of them.

ol: Tap on the face to set focus and exposure there. The phone brightens the image for that point.
If the sky turns pure white, drag the brightness or exposure slider (the sun icon on iPhone) down a little. If the face is still dark, drag it up.
Lock it so the phone does not readjust while you recompose: press and hold on iPhone for AE/AF Lock, or tap the Lock button on Pixel.
Leave HDR or smart HDR on. Phones merge several frames to keep the sky and the face, which works well for still subjects.
For a silhouette, tap on the bright sky instead, and lower exposure until the subject is black.
Use the 2x or 3x lens and portrait mode for a soft, bright background with lights turned into circles.
Wipe the lens. Fingerprint grease on a phone lens turns backlight into a milky haze across the whole image.

body: Flare appears as colored shapes, streaks or a washed-out, low-contrast look when bright light hits the lens directly. A little haze can feel warm and dreamy. Too much hides the subject.

ul: Use a lens hood, or shade the front of the lens with your hand or a card just outside the frame.
Hide the sun partly behind the subject, a tree or a building edge.
Remove cheap filters; extra glass adds reflections.
Move a few centimeters. Flare shapes move and change as the angle changes.
Keep the lens clean. Dust and grease make flare much worse.
For a sunstar, use f/11 to f/16 and let the edge of the sun just peek past an object.

body.note: Never look at the sun through an optical viewfinder or a long lens, even briefly. Compose on the rear screen, and do not leave any camera or phone pointed at the sun for long periods.

faq.a: Yes, when you control the exposure. Backlight gives soft light on the face, no squinting, and a glowing outline in the hair. You only need to expose for the face or add some fill light.

faq.q: Why are my photos dark when I shoot toward a window?
faq.a: The bright window makes the camera reduce exposure for the whole frame. Tap on the person to expose for them, raise the exposure slider, or move so the window is beside them instead of behind.

faq.q: What is the difference between backlight and rim light?
faq.a: Backlight is any light from behind the subject. Rim light is the bright edge it creates on hair, shoulders or the outline of an object, usually when the light is behind and slightly to the side.

faq.q: How do I get a sunstar effect?
faq.a: Use a small aperture such as f/11 to f/16 and let only a small part of the sun show past an edge. Lenses with an even number of aperture blades give as many rays as blades; odd numbers give twice as many.

faq.q: Should I use HDR for backlit photos?
faq.a: On a phone, yes for still subjects, because it blends several exposures to keep both the sky and the face. With fast movement, HDR can blur or ghost, so a single frame with fill light may be better.
